title: Contact Group 51/49: Pale's Response
sources: UNSCR 942 (23 September 1994) — Contact Group plan sanctions on the RS
content:
In July 1994 the Contact Group presented its 51/49 territorial framework to the Bosnian Serb leadership on a take-it-or-leave-it basis. The map required the RS to cede territory toward the 49 percent line — narrowing the Posavina corridor, dividing the Drina valley, and surrendering the claim to a unified Serb capital in a partitioned Sarajevo.

Slobodan Milošević, by then desperate to lift the sanctions strangling the Serbian economy, signalled Belgrade's willingness to accept and pressed Pale to do the same. The Karadžić judgment records the assembly that convened at Bijeljina on 3 August 1994 and rejected the plan, against Belgrade's wishes. The rejection triggered exactly the consequence the Contact Group had designed: Milošević closed the Drina border to the RS in August 1994 and submitted to international monitoring of the closure, rupturing the Belgrade-Pale axis that had sustained the Bosnian Serb war effort.

UNSCR 942 codified the Contact Group's coercion, extending sanctions specifically against the RS for its rejection. The choice Pale faced was therefore between accepting a map that banked its gains at the cost of its maximal claims, rejecting it and absorbing the Belgrade rupture, or negotiating amendments to soften the territorial concessions.

The posture recorded here determines whether the RS entered 1995 with Belgrade behind it or isolated — the single variable that most shaped its collapse under Operation Storm and Deliberate Force.
